title: Stocks edge higher as Treasury yields steady ahead of Fed meeting
summary: The S&P 500 posted a modest gain Thursday as investors digested the latest batch of earnings and looked ahead to next week's policy meeting.
body: U.S. equities finished modestly higher on Thursday, with the S&P 500 up 0.3% and the Nasdaq Composite adding 0.5%, as bond yields eased off their morning highs.
Energy shares lagged after crude inventories came in above expectations, while technology and financials led the advance.
Attention now shifts to the Federal Reserve's two-day meeting beginning Tuesday. Futures markets are pricing roughly a 60% chance of a quarter-point cut.
"The market has been remarkably resilient this month," said one strategist. "The question is whether that holds once the Fed decision is behind us."

title: S&P 500 notches third straight weekly gain
summary: A quiet Friday session was enough to extend the index's winning streak, capping a 1.8% gain for the week.
body: The S&P 500 closed out its third consecutive weekly advance Friday, finishing the week up 1.8%.
Volume was light ahead of the weekend, and volatility stayed subdued with the VIX holding below 15.
Broad-market ETFs saw another week of net inflows, extending what has been the strongest stretch of the year for index fund demand.
Next week brings a full slate of earnings along with the Fed's rate decision and the monthly jobs report.

title: Fed officials signal patience on rate path as inflation cools
summary: Several policymakers suggested they see no urgency to move quickly, even as core inflation drifts back toward the 2% target.
body: Federal Reserve officials offered a patient tone in a series of public appearances this week, signaling comfort with the current policy stance.
Core inflation has cooled for four consecutive months and now sits at 2.3% year over year, close to the central bank's long-run goal.
"The last mile of disinflation is behind us; the question now is the neutral rate," one governor said at a banking conference.
Economists still expect one more cut this year, though timing remains split between December and early next year.

title: Jobless claims fall to five-month low, pointing to resilient labor market
summary: Initial unemployment claims dropped to 213,000 last week, the lowest reading since May.
body: New applications for unemployment benefits fell to 213,000 last week, a five-month low and the latest sign the labor market remains on solid footing.
Continuing claims also edged lower, suggesting laid-off workers are finding new roles quickly.
The report bolsters the soft-landing narrative that has supported equity valuations through the second half of the year.
Attention turns to next Friday's payrolls report, with consensus looking for a gain of 145,000 jobs.

title: Why maxing out your IRA contributions early matters
summary: Front-loading your annual contribution gives your money more time in the market, and the math is more powerful than most people expect.
body: Most investors wait until tax season to fund their IRA. But contributing in January instead of April gives your money up to 15 extra months of tax-advantaged compounding every year.
Over a 30-year career, that head start can add tens of thousands of dollars to your balance, purely from the extra time in the market.
If a lump sum feels out of reach, automatic monthly contributions are a perfectly good alternative and help smooth out market timing.
Check your contribution limits each year, especially if you turn 50 and become eligible for catch-up contributions.

title: Catch-up contributions: what changes at age 50
summary: The year you turn 50 you unlock higher contribution limits across 401(k)s and IRAs. Here is how the numbers stack up.
body: Once you reach age 50, the IRS lets you contribute extra amounts to your retirement accounts under what are known as catch-up provisions.
For workplace plans, the catch-up can add thousands of dollars a year above the standard employee limit, and older workers within three years of retirement may qualify for even larger amounts.
The extra room compounds quickly: an additional $7,000 a year invested for 15 years at a 7% return grows to roughly $175,000.
If cash flow is tight, prioritize any employer match first, then direct raises and bonuses toward the catch-up room.

title: High-yield savings rates hold above 4% as banks compete for deposits
summary: Even as the Fed debates further cuts, the best savings rates have barely budged. Competition for household deposits remains fierce.
body: Top-yielding savings accounts continue to pay north of 4% APY, a level that has held steady for most of the year.
Analysts attribute the stickiness to banks competing aggressively for household deposits as loan growth picks up.
For savers, the advice is simple: if your account pays materially less than 4%, it has never been easier to switch.
Watch for promotional rates that drop after an introductory period, and confirm the rate is variable before parking your emergency fund.

title: Debit card skimming is on the rise: 6 habits that keep you safer
summary: Skimming devices were up double digits this year. A few simple habits dramatically cut your exposure.
body: Reports of debit card skimming were up double digits in the first half of the year, with gas pumps and standalone ATMs remaining the most common targets.
Prefer ATMs inside bank branches or well-lit, high-traffic locations, and give the card reader a tug before inserting your card.
Enable transaction alerts so you learn about fraudulent activity in minutes, not weeks. Turning your card off between purchases takes seconds in most mobile apps.
If you do spot an unfamiliar charge, freeze the card immediately and report it, unauthorized debit transactions are generally covered when reported promptly.

title: Index funds vs. actively managed funds: the fee drag, visualized
summary: A one percent fee gap sounds small. Over a 40-year career it quietly consumes a quarter of a portfolio's growth.
body: The average actively managed mutual fund charges roughly 0.6% more per year than a comparable index fund.
That difference compounds relentlessly. On a $500,000 portfolio earning 7% annually, a 1% fee consumes about $580,000 of potential growth over 30 years.
Active managers do occasionally beat their benchmarks, but the percentage that does so over 15 years is small and difficult to identify in advance.
The pragmatic approach for most savers: index the core of the portfolio and, if you want active exposure, cap it at a small slice.

title: Dividend investing 101: building a paycheck from your portfolio
summary: Dividend funds have attracted record flows this year. Here is how payouts actually reach your account.
body: Dividend investing is having a moment: funds focused on dividend payers have seen record inflows over the past twelve months.
Companies that pay dividends distribute a portion of earnings to shareholders quarterly, and dividend ETFs pass those payouts through after expenses.
Two numbers matter most: the yield, which tells you the income relative to price today, and the growth rate, which tells you how fast the payout has been rising.
Reinvested dividends are one of the most reliable compounding engines available to a long-term investor. Payouts can be reduced or suspended, so diversification matters.

title: Nvidia leads chip rally as datacenter capex forecasts climb
summary: Semiconductor shares jumped after two hyperscalers raised their infrastructure spending guidance.
body: Chip stocks rallied Thursday after a pair of large cloud providers raised their datacenter capital expenditure forecasts for next year.
Nvidia gained more than 3%, extending its lead as the best-performing mega cap of the year.
The move lifted the broader semiconductor complex, with equipment makers and memory suppliers also posting strong sessions.
Skeptics continue to flag the concentration risk, the top five stocks in the S&P 500 now account for nearly 30% of the index weight.

title: Treasury auction sees strong demand for 10-year notes
summary: Indirect bids came in well above average, sending yields lower and easing pressure on rate-sensitive sectors.
body: The Treasury's auction of 10-year notes drew strong demand, with indirect bidders taking down the highest share in eight months.
The yield on the benchmark 10-year slipped to 4.02% in afternoon trading, a two-week low.
Solid auction results have helped keep long-end volatility in check, even as the Fed deliberates its next move.
Mortgage rates, which track the 10-year closely, fell back below 6.3% this week, a small relief for prospective homebuyers.
